unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 3 is called Reflections because it asks you to look closely at the world and say what you see, think and feel. You will read a rhyming river poem, three haiku and a reflective passage about the wind, and you will meet figurative language: simile, metaphor and personification. The story 'The Cracked Charter' takes the same skill into a museum mystery about a town charter with a crack running through it. The grammar focus is comparative and superlative adjectives, which you will use to compare poems, texts and ideas in your own reflective writing.
unit.learningPath:
1. Vocabulary: learn the six word groups a few words at a time and tick your Word Wall.
2. Reading and story: read 'The River', the three haiku, 'Looking at the Wind' and both parts of 'The Cracked Charter'.
3. Comprehension: answer the twelve questions and quote the line that proves each answer.
4. Grammar: work through the six comparative and superlative lessons and their practice.
5. Activities: hunt for figurative language, compare the poems, and complete the theme and tone chart.
6. Writing: draft a haiku, a simile poem, a reflective paragraph and a comparison paragraph.
7. Speaking: perform choral verse, interview the poet and debate the cracked charter.
8. Quiz and My progress: take the checkpoint quiz, then rate yourself on the six statements.

readings.title: The River
readings.setting: A river beside a familiar town
readings.passageScript:
The River

The river is a silver traveller,
Restless, never still.
He hurries past the sleeping town,
He whispers to the hill.
He gossips with the bending reeds,
He argues with the stones,
And all night long beneath the bridge
He mutters and he moans.

But when the heavy rains arrive
The traveller starts to roar.
He shoulders through the narrow arch,
He hammers at the shore,
He drags the branches from the bank,
He shakes the willow trees,
And shouts a wild and muddy song
To every wind that flees.

Then April brings a quieter light
And all his temper goes.
He stretches out along the fields
And, drowsy, almost dozes.
The dragonflies go stitching past,
The reeds forget to sway,
And Amal, sitting on the wall,
Sees him grow gentler every day.

— Ehel Academy poetry collection

Read the poem twice: once silently, once aloud. The first line is a metaphor. The poet says the river is a traveller, rather than comparing it with like or as. Almost every other line is personification, because the river whispers, gossips, argues, mutters, shouts and dozes. Notice how the tone changes: stanza one is playful, stanza two is wild, stanza three is calm.

readings.title: Three Haiku for a Year
readings.passageScript:
Three Haiku for a Year

A haiku is a very short Japanese poem with a strict syllable pattern. The first line has five syllables, the second has seven, and the third has five again. Haiku usually describe something in nature and end with a surprising image or comparison.

Haiku 1: Penguins
Penguins, black and white
March across the frozen sea,
Small and patient kings.

Clap it out: Pen-guins, black, and, white. That first line holds five syllables, and the last line calls the birds kings, which is a metaphor.

Haiku 2: Lava
Boiling orange rock
Climbing from the mountain top,
Eager to be free.

Rock cannot climb and rock cannot be eager, so both of those lines are personification. The poet gives the lava a wish of its own.

Haiku 3: Dew
Cool morning dew drops
Resting on the spider web,
Nature's silver rings.

The last line is a metaphor: the drops are not like rings, they are called rings. Count the syllables in every line and check the five, seven, five pattern for yourself.

— Ehel Academy poetry collection

A haiku is far shorter than the river poem, and it holds one picture rather than a whole story. That is why poets say a haiku must choose its words more carefully than any other form.

readings.title: Looking at the Wind
readings.setting: A neighbourhood courtyard on a windy day
readings.passageScript:
Looking at the Wind

I remember the day the wind came to our neighbourhood like an uninvited guest. It arrived without warning, lifting the dust from the streets and hurling it against our windows. The old acacia tree in the courtyard trembled and bent, as though it were bowing to a powerful king. Sheets of laundry flew from the line like startled birds.

My little sister Mina hid under the table with her eyes wide open. "Is the wind angry?" she whispered. I told her the wind was not angry. It was only doing its work, pushing clouds across the sky so the rain could follow. Secretly, though, I thought the wind did sound angry that day. It howled between the buildings and rattled every door in the street.

When it stopped, the world was quiet in a way I had never noticed before. The leaves lay still. The dust settled. Everything looked washed and new, as if the wind had swept our whole neighbourhood clean. I stepped outside and breathed in the cool air. Mother called me in for supper, but I stood there a moment longer, feeling grateful. Even something wild and frightening can leave the world more beautiful than it found it.

This is a reflection. The writer describes what happened, admits how she felt, and then shares a bigger thought at the end.

readings.title: The Cracked Charter, part 1
readings.setting: An old town courthouse and museum
readings.passageScript:
The Cracked Charter, part 1

In our town an old courthouse stands beside a small museum. The walls are dusty and the sign outside has faded. Inside, though, a Year 5 class stood in complete silence. They had come for a history project, and they were about to solve something nobody expected.

Teacher Yasmin led them into a quiet hall. "This building once held debates," she said. "People argued about policy here, voted on rules, and wrote the first drafts of our town constitution."

Amal walked slowly across the tiled floor. "It smells like paper and time," she whispered.

Nora pointed to a glass case in the centre of the room. "Look. That is the original town charter."

The page inside was yellow with age and sealed behind thick protective glass.

Sami leaned closer. "There is a fracture in it," he said. "A line runs right through the middle of the page."

"That is strange," said Teacher Yasmin. "Let us ask the curator."

They found the curator in the lobby, sorting labels for a new display of artefacts.

"Why is there a crack in the charter?" asked Amal.

The curator smiled. "That is part of the story. Some people say the town council had a fracture in trust. A disagreement broke their unity on the very day the charter was signed."

"May we study it for our project?" Amal asked.

"You may," the curator said. "But treat it with care. It is an artefact, and the protective glass around it is nearly as old as the page itself."

The class began to sketch the charter and read the labels around the case. Suddenly Nora gasped.

"This stamp is not from our town."

Teacher Yasmin looked closely. "You are right. That symbol is legislative. It belonged to the regional capital, not to us."

"Then why is their symbol on our charter?" asked Sami.

The curator nodded slowly. "Now that is a question worth asking."

readings.title: The Cracked Charter, part 2
readings.setting: An old town courthouse and museum
readings.passageScript:
The Cracked Charter, part 2

The next week the class turned the mystery into a mission. They split into groups. One group researched the history of the local government. Another studied the architects who had built the first miniature model of the courthouse.

"Listen to this," said Amal. "One of the architects lobbied for a bigger hall. He wanted more public voices at every meeting."

"But the mayor of that time preferred small rooms," said Sami. "He warned that tension in a crowded hall could spread like an infection."

"That is a weak argument," said Nora. "Fear of expansion is not a reason to silence people."

Teacher Yasmin nodded. "Use that in your report. It is an opinion built on a careful comprehension of history."

On presentation day the class covered the wall with maps, notes and a collaborative mural of voices breaking through a cracked wall.

"We believe the fracture in the charter is both real and symbolic," Nora explained. "It shows the argument between people who wanted tradition and people who asked for change."

"Some of them feared any alternative policy," Sami added. "But a town works better when its ideas are shared."

The class used comparatives to show that modern rules are more inclusive than the earliest ones. They used a superlative too: today's constitution is the most protective the town has ever had.

Everyone clapped. That afternoon the mayor visited.

"You have opened a new dimension to an old problem," she said.

"May we suggest ideas for a youth charter?" Amal asked.

"You may," said the mayor. "Write one. Let it show what your generation hopes for."

Over the next week the class wrote together. Nora typed the opening: "We believe nobody is too small to speak. Our mission is to learn, to listen and to lead." Amal added a promise about tradition: "We will value every tradition, but we will not let one block progress." Sami closed it: "Our system must be fairer, clearer and more competitive in ideas, never in anger."

They called it The Students' Charter of Hope.

On the final day the mayor returned. The class stood straight, and their posture showed how proud they were.

"One day some of you may serve in our legislative halls," she said.

"And I will design them," said Amal. "I want to be an architect."

"And I will guard them like a vulture," said Sami.

Teacher Yasmin laughed kindly. "A vulture cleans up after other animals, Sami. Choose an eagle if you want a guard."

"You function well as a team," the mayor said. "That is the most powerful kind of constitution."

The cracked charter stayed in its case, but now it meant something new. It was no longer only a broken page. It was a lesson: even a fracture can lead to a stronger foundation.

comprehension.question: In 'The River', the poet writes that the river is a silver traveller. Is that a simile or a metaphor, and how can you tell?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It is a metaphor, because the poet says the river is a traveller instead of comparing it with like or as.
comprehension.explanation: A simile needs the words like or as. This line states the comparison directly, which makes it a metaphor.

comprehension.question: Name two human actions the river performs in the first stanza of 'The River'.
comprehension.correctAnswer: The river whispers to the hill, gossips with the bending reeds, argues with the stones and mutters beneath the bridge.
comprehension.explanation: Whispering, gossiping, arguing and muttering are things people do, so giving them to a river is personification.

comprehension.question: How does the tone of 'The River' change between the second and third stanzas? Quote one word from each stanza as evidence.
comprehension.correctAnswer: The second stanza is wild, shown by the word shouts, while the third is calm, shown by the word dozes.
comprehension.explanation: Tone is the feeling a writer creates, and the poet signals the change by swapping loud verbs for sleepy ones.

comprehension.question: Count the syllables in each line of the penguin haiku. Does it follow the five, seven, five pattern?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Yes. Penguins, black and white has five syllables, March across the frozen sea has seven, and Small and patient kings has five.
comprehension.explanation: Clapping each line is the quickest way to check a haiku, because one clap marks one vowel sound.

comprehension.question: In the dew haiku the drops are called Nature's silver rings. Is that literal or figurative language, and what is being compared?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It is figurative, because the dew drops are not really rings; their round shine is compared with jewellery.
comprehension.explanation: Literal language means exactly what it says, while figurative language asks the reader to picture something else.

comprehension.question: Find the simile that describes how the wind arrived in 'Looking at the Wind', and explain what it tells you.
comprehension.correctAnswer: The wind came like an uninvited guest, which shows that it arrived suddenly and was not welcome.
comprehension.explanation: The word like signals a simile, and an uninvited guest carries the idea of rudeness and surprise together.

comprehension.question: What does Mina do when the wind reaches the house, and what question does she ask her older sister?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Mina hides under the table with her eyes wide open and asks whether the wind is angry.
comprehension.explanation: Her hiding shows fear before she speaks, so the action and the question together prove how frightened she is.

comprehension.question: What did Sami notice about the charter inside the glass case?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Sami noticed a fracture, a line running right through the middle of the page.
comprehension.explanation: The word fracture means a break or crack, and Sami is the first character to name it aloud.

comprehension.question: Why was the stamp on the charter surprising to the class?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The symbol was legislative and belonged to the regional capital, so it should not have been on their town charter.
comprehension.explanation: Teacher Yasmin identifies the symbol, and the surprise comes from a document carrying another authority's mark.

comprehension.question: What does the curator mean when she says the town council had a fracture in trust?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She means a disagreement broke the council's unity, just as a crack breaks a page in two.
comprehension.explanation: The curator borrows a physical word for a feeling, which is exactly how figurative language works.

comprehension.question: What did the old mayor fear about a bigger hall, and why did Nora call that a weak argument?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He feared tension would spread like an infection, but Nora said fear of expansion cannot justify silencing people.
comprehension.explanation: The mayor's worry is an opinion rather than evidence, which is why Nora is able to challenge it.

comprehension.question: Why does Teacher Yasmin gently correct Sami's comparison with a vulture?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A vulture cleans up after other animals rather than guarding, so an eagle is the more accurate image.
comprehension.explanation: A comparison only works when it matches the real thing, so an inaccurate image weakens the writing.

grammar.title: What Comparatives and Superlatives Do
grammar.explanation: Comparatives and superlatives are special forms of adjectives that let you weigh one thing against another. A comparative measures exactly two things; a superlative ranks one thing against a whole group of three or more.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A comparative compares TWO things and almost always brings the word than with it.
"A haiku is shorter than a ballad."
"The river poem is wilder than the third haiku."
A superlative compares THREE OR MORE things and almost always brings the word the with it.
"She is the best poet in our class."
"Today's constitution is the most protective the town has ever had."
Both forms come from ordinary adjectives, so start by finding the adjective: short, wild, good, protective.
You will use both forms whenever you compare poems, characters, places or ideas in your writing.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: using a superlative when only two things are being weighed, as in "Of my two poems, this one is the best." Fix: two things need a comparative, so write "Of my two poems, this one is better."
grammar.memoryTip: Two things take than; three or more take the. Say "than for two, the for the whole crew" before you choose a form.
grammar.practice: Part A. Read these four lines from 'The Cracked Charter'. grammar.title: Forming Comparatives: -er, -ier and more
grammar.explanation: Three simple rules cover almost every comparative in English, and which rule you use depends only on how many syllables the adjective has and how it is spelt.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Rule 1 — one-syllable adjectives: add -er.
tall becomes taller: "The tree is taller than the house."
fast becomes faster: "Nora ran faster than Sami."
old becomes older: "The charter is older than the museum."
Spelling note: if the adjective ends in one vowel plus one consonant, double the last consonant. big becomes bigger, hot becomes hotter, sad becomes sadder.
Rule 2 — adjectives ending in -y: change the y to i, then add -er.
happy becomes happier: "She felt happier after the presentation."
easy becomes easier: "The second exercise was easier than the first."
funny becomes funnier: "His joke was funnier than mine."
Rule 3 — adjectives of two or more syllables: put more in front and leave the adjective alone.
beautiful becomes more beautiful: "The sunset was more beautiful than yesterday's."
inclusive becomes more inclusive: "Our rules are more inclusive than the old ones."
competitive becomes more competitive: "The debate was more competitive this year."
Always add than when you name both of the things you are comparing: "Poetry is more creative than a report."
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: dropping than, as in "She is taller me." Fix: name both sides of the comparison and join them with than, so write "She is taller than me."
grammar.memoryTip: Count the syllables first. One syllable takes -er, an adjective ending in -y swaps that y for an i, and anything longer borrows more.
grammar.practice: Part A. Write the correct comparative form of the adjective in brackets. | This book is __________ (interesting) than the last one. | My brother's handwriting is __________ (neat) than mine. | This exercise is __________ (easy) than Exercise 1. | Part B. Part B: 1) shorter, 2) wilder, 3) more inclusive, 4) more confident, 5) more difficult.

grammar.title: Forming Superlatives: -est, -iest and the most
grammar.explanation: Superlatives follow the same three-way pattern as comparatives, with one extra habit: the word the almost always stands in front of them.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Rule 1 — one-syllable adjectives: add -est and put the in front.
tall becomes the tallest: "She is the tallest girl in the class."
fast becomes the fastest: "He is the fastest runner in the school."
old becomes the oldest: "That is the oldest building in town."
Spelling note: the doubling rule applies here too. big becomes the biggest, hot becomes the hottest.
Rule 2 — adjectives ending in -y: change the y to i, add -est, and put the in front.
happy becomes the happiest: "That was the happiest day of my life."
easy becomes the easiest: "This was the easiest question on the test."
pretty becomes the prettiest: "She wore the prettiest dress."
Rule 3 — adjectives of two or more syllables: use the most and leave the adjective alone.
beautiful becomes the most beautiful: "That is the most beautiful poem I have ever read."
protective becomes the most protective: "Our constitution is the most protective we have had."
exciting becomes the most exciting: "That was the most exciting presentation."
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: leaving out the, as in "He is fastest runner." Fix: a superlative points to one winner in a group, so it needs the: "He is the fastest runner."
grammar.memoryTip: A superlative is a prize-giving, and every prize has one winner, so hand it the before you say it: the tallest, the happiest, the most protective.
grammar.practice: Part A. Write the correct superlative form of the adjective in brackets. | Mount Kilimanjaro is __________ (tall) mountain in Africa. | A cheetah is __________ (fast) land animal. | He told __________ (funny) joke in the whole school. | Part B. Complete each sentence with the correct superlative. | That was __________ (exciting) poem I have ever read. | The wind was __________ (strong) force of nature that day. | This is __________ (beautiful) haiku in the collection. | Part C. Write two superlative sentences of your own about the three haiku you read. | Answer key (self-check) — Part A: 1) the tallest, 2) the fastest, 3) the funniest. Part C is open-ended, so there is no fixed answer — instead, check your two sentences against this model example: "The penguin haiku is the most patient of the three." / "The lava haiku is the fiercest poem in the set." Make sure each sentence truly ranks all three haiku (not just two) and uses "the" plus "-est" or "the most" plus a longer adjective.

grammar.title: Irregular Comparatives and Superlatives
grammar.explanation: A small group of very common adjectives refuses to follow the rules and changes shape completely. There is no pattern to work out, so these forms have to be learned by heart.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
good becomes better, then best: "She is a better writer than I am." (never gooder)
bad becomes worse, then worst: "That was the worst storm in years." (never the most bad)
far becomes farther or further, then farthest or furthest: "The school is farther than the library."
much and many become more, then most: "He has more books than anyone." (never mucher)
little becomes less, then least: "She ate the least food at dinner." (never the most little)
These five entries cover nearly every irregular comparison a Grade 5 writer needs.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: forcing the regular endings on to an irregular word, as in "My drawing is gooder than yours." Fix: swap in the memorised form: "My drawing is better than yours."
grammar.memoryTip: Learn them as five short chants: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; far, farther, farthest; much, more, most; little, less, least.
grammar.practice: Part A. Write the correct irregular form of the adjective in brackets. | She is __________ (good) at maths than at English. | That was __________ (bad) film I have ever watched. | She is __________ (good) poet in our school. | He wrote __________ (bad) essay in the class, but he improved next time. | This is __________ (bad) meal I have ever tasted. | Part B. Part B is open-ended, so there is no single correct sentence — check yours against this model example instead: "My drawing is better than it was last month." Make sure you used "better," never "gooder." Part C is also open-ended — check yours against this model example: "That was the worst mistake I have ever made in a spelling test." Make sure you used "the worst," never "the baddest."

grammar.title: Five Comparison Mistakes and How to Fix Them
grammar.explanation: Almost every comparison error a Grade 5 writer makes belongs to one of five families. Learn to spot the family and the repair is quick.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
1. Double comparative — do not use -er and more together.
Wrong: "She is more taller than her sister." Correct: "She is taller than her sister."
2. Missing the in a superlative — always put the in front.
Wrong: "He is fastest runner." Correct: "He is the fastest runner."
3. Long adjective with -est — never bolt -est on to a long adjective.
Wrong: "This is the beautifulest poem." Correct: "This is the most beautiful poem."
4. Wrong irregular form — do not add -er or -est to an irregular adjective.
Wrong: "My drawing is gooder than yours." Correct: "My drawing is better than yours."
5. Missing than — include than whenever you name both things.
Wrong: "She is taller me." Correct: "She is taller than me."
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: piling the most on top of an -est ending, as in "the most biggest building". Fix: choose one marker only and keep the shorter form: "the biggest building".
grammar.memoryTip: Ask three quick questions of every comparison you write: have I marked it twice, have I forgotten the, and have I forgotten than?

Part B: 1) "She is taller than her sister." 2) "He is the fastest runner in the team." 3) "This poem is the most beautiful I have read." 4) "My handwriting is better now than last term." 5) "That was the worst storm in ten years." Part C: 1) bigger, 2) the most exciting, 3) more careful, 4) the worst, 5) more beautiful, 6) the fastest, 7) hotter, 8) the happiest.

grammar.title: Using Comparisons in Your Own Reflective Writing
grammar.explanation: Comparisons earn their place when they carry meaning. A reflective writer uses them to show change, to rank an opinion and to explain why one text moved them more than another.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Build a comparison in three steps. First name the two things. Second choose the adjective that really matters. Third pick the right form.
"The rainy season is more colourful than the dry season."
"The grass grows greener than an emerald."
"The sky is at its most beautiful when the sun breaks through after a storm."
When you edit, read the paragraph aloud and check one feature at a time: sentence completeness, the comparative or superlative form, punctuation, then the joining words.
A comparison that changes nothing should be cut. Keep the ones that let the reader see a difference.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: stacking so many comparisons into one paragraph that none of them lands. Fix: keep the two or three that carry real meaning and delete the rest.
grammar.memoryTip: Name the two things, choose the adjective that matters, then pick the form. Name, choose, form.
grammar.practice: Part A. Write one sentence for each instruction. | Use a comparative to compare two fruits. | Use a superlative to say which animal is the best climber. | Use more plus a long adjective to compare two places. | Use the most plus a long adjective to describe your favourite poem of this unit. | Compare two animals you know, using a comparative. | Say which food is the best in your family, using a superlative. | Compare your favourite poem from this unit with another, using a comparative. | Describe the most beautiful place you have seen, using a superlative. | Part B. Write a short paragraph of five to eight sentences comparing two seasons. It must contain at least two comparatives, at least one superlative, and one simile or metaphor. | Part C. Edit your paragraph. Mark four changes and explain in writing how two of them improved the meaning. | Answer key (self-check): every part of this practice asks for your own original writing, so there is no single fixed answer for any part — use these model examples to check your work instead. Part A models (one per instruction, in order): "A mango is sweeter than a lemon." / "A monkey is the best climber of all the animals in the forest." / "The city is more crowded than the village." / "'The River' is the most reflective poem in this unit." / "A cheetah is faster than a tortoise." / "Grandma's bread is the tastiest food in our family." / "My haiku is shorter than 'The River.'" / "The mountain view was the most beautiful place I have ever seen." Check that each of your own sentences names the right number of things (two for a comparative, three or more for a superlative) and includes "than" or "the" correctly. Part B model paragraph: "Summer feels louder than winter in our street. In summer the loudest sound is laughter from open windows, but winter is quieter and calmer. The bare trees stand like tired old men waiting for spring. I think summer is livelier than winter, yet winter is the cosiest season of the year because everyone gathers close together. Winter's silence is more comforting than summer's noise, and its snow looks like a soft white blanket over the whole town." Check that your own paragraph has at least two comparatives, at least one superlative, and one simile or metaphor. Part C self-check: reread your paragraph aloud, mark four changes, and write two sentences explaining how two of those changes improved the meaning — there is no fixed correct edit, so check only that each explanation names what changed and why it helps the reader.

writing.title: Writing 3: Reflective Paragraph

writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a reflective paragraph of eight to twelve sentences about a time when something in nature surprised you or made you think. writing.modelText: A first-person paragraph that moves from scene, to feeling, to figurative image, to reflection, and closes with an honest thought rather than a summary.
writing.sentenceStarter: I still remember the day when...

items: I still remember the afternoon the sky turned dark before I even reached my gate. I had been walking home from school under a clear, hot sky. I never imagined rain in the middle of the dry season.

At first the clouds rolling in like a grey wave frightened me. Cold, fat drops fell against my hot skin, and the wind pulled at my school bag. Then, as the rain settled into a steady rhythm, my fear slowly turned into wonder.
The dusty street became a mirror, reflecting the grey clouds above it. Under the mango tree I watched the dry earth drink every drop it had been missing for months.
I learned that an unexpected change can be a gift rather than a disaster.

Now, whenever I feel the first cold drop of rain, I remember that afternoon and smile instead of worrying, because that short, surprising storm taught me to look for the good hidden inside a sudden change.

writing.promptAndInstructions: Choose one of these three tasks about 'The Cracked Charter'. Write your own youth charter setting out five rules you believe matter for young people. Or write a letter to the mayor of your town. Suggest one change you would like to see, and give two reasons for it. Or imagine you are Amal, Nora or Sami. Write a diary entry about the day you discovered the mystery of the cracked charter. Whichever you choose, use at least four unit words.
writing.modelText: A response that keeps the form it chose: a charter reads as numbered promises, a letter opens and closes politely, and a diary entry stays in first person and in the past tense.

items: Dear Diary, today our class visited the old courthouse and museum for our history project, and I never expected to find a real mystery inside.
The room smelled of paper and time, and behind protective glass we saw the original town charter, an artefact yellow with age.
Sami noticed a fracture running right through the middle of the page, and when we asked the curator about it, she told us it might show a fracture in the old council's trust.
Then Nora spotted something even stranger: a legislative stamp from the regional capital, not from our own town, stamped onto our charter.
I felt a strange tension in my chest, half excitement and half worry, because a small crack in a page seemed to be hiding a much bigger question about our town's history.
Tonight I keep wondering why another town's authority ever touched our charter, and I cannot wait to start our research and build my comprehension of what really happened that day.
Whatever the answer turns out to be, I know this mission has already changed how I look at the cracked page in that glass case.
otherAnswers: Instead of a diary entry, a valid response could be a five-rule youth charter beginning 'We believe...' and covering fairness, voice, learning, respect and courage.
A valid response could also be a polite letter to the mayor suggesting one change, such as adding more youth representatives to town meetings, backed by two clear reasons.

writing.promptAndInstructions: Swap your haiku or simile poem with a partner or your adult helper if one is available, or read your own poem back to yourself. Answer four questions about the work in writing (your partner’s, or your own if you are alone). Does the haiku follow the five, seven, five pattern? Can you find a simile, a metaphor or personification in the poem? Which is the strongest line, and why? Use a superlative. What single change would make the poem more vivid? Use a comparative. Then revise your own poem using the feedback you received and explain one change you made.
writing.modelText: Feedback that names a specific line rather than praising the whole poem, followed by a revision that shows exactly what the writer changed and why.
writing.sentenceStarter: The strongest line in this poem is...
writing.expectedLength: Four written answers plus one revision

items: Question 1 (five, seven, five pattern): Yes — my partner Idil's haiku keeps the pattern exactly: five syllables, then seven, then five.
Question 2 (simile, metaphor or personification): Yes, 'like a thousand drums' is a simile that compares the sound of the rain to drumming.
Question 3 (strongest line, using a superlative): The second line is the strongest line in the poem, because 'taps gently on the roof' lets the reader hear the rain instead of only picturing it.

Question 4 (one change, using a comparative): Line one could be more specific than 'grey clouds gather fast' — naming the colour and shape of the clouds would help the picture form faster in the reader's mind.
My revised poem: A round silver moon / climbs slowly above the hill, / a coin dropped in ink.

The change I made: I replaced my first draft's plain line, 'The moon is in the sky,' with 'A round silver moon,' because Idil's feedback reminded me that a clear, literal image works better than a vague statement.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Reflections" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 9-10 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'policy'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Identify and explain similes, metaphors and personification in poems.
Read and compare different kinds of poetry, including haiku and rhyming verse.
Count syllables and explain how poets use rhythm, sound and line length.
Tell the difference between literal and figurative language in a text.
Describe the theme and tone of a poem or reflective text in your own words.
Form and use comparative and superlative adjectives correctly in your writing.
Write a reflective poem and a reflective paragraph that use figurative language.
Perform a poem aloud with expression and give a classmate useful feedback.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "The Cracked Charter, part 1" was about in their own words — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "What Comparatives and Superlatives Do" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.

sections.title: Sentence Patterns to Say Out Loud
items: A comparative compares TWO things and almost always brings the word than with it.
The tree is taller than the house.
She is the tallest girl in the class.
She is a better writer than I am.
She is taller than her sister.
Build a comparison in three steps.

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. These are the signs the unit has landed — listen for them in conversation and look for them in the writing:
items: Activities 1 and comprehension answers name a simile, a metaphor and a personification with the line that proves each.
Activities 2 compares 'The River' with the haiku collection for length, structure and figurative language.
Writing 1 produces a haiku with a checked five, seven, five pattern, and Speaking 5 records an accurate dictation.
Activities 4 gives a context-clue definition for five words and states which clue helped most.
Activities 3 completes a seven-row theme and tone chart with a proof word for every row.
Writing 4 contains at least two comparatives and one superlative, and the grammar practice is corrected without help.
Writing 2 and Writing 3 are drafted, revised after peer feedback, and include named figurative devices.
Speaking 1 is recorded as choral verse, and Writing 6 returns four specific feedback comments to a partner.
